title: Two months from first commit to Google Play with Claude Code agents: what worked, and where a human still had to play it
author: Andy12100
selftext:
Trundleway is a cozy truck game for Android: you haul freight on real motorways between real cities in Austria, Germany, Hungary and Luxembourg, then back the trailer into the dock. It went public this week. First commit was 25 September. The code is written by Claude Code agents; my part is the design, the taste, the playtesting and saying no a lot. Here is what I learned, because the game itself is the less interesting part for this sub.
    
    The thing that worked best: a reference to prove against. The game started as a web game (three.js). When it could not hold 60 fps on old phones, the agents rewrote it as a native game in Rust on a small engine of our own. From the first line of Rust to the public release took about nine days, and the reason it was not a disaster is that the web version stayed in the repo as the spec. The simulation is deterministic, so the Rust one is compared with the JavaScript one frame by frame, and the menus page by page. "Looks right" was never the test.
    
    Second: the AI writes its own manual. There is a guide file in the repo, 13,000 lines by now, that every agent reads parts of and updates in the same commit as the code: what was built, how it was proved, what is still not verified. Plus a short rules file from me (a cap on how many agents run at once, written after I exhausted my usage limit twice, one heavy job on the machine at a time, "fix it as a rule with a test, never as a one-place patch").
    
    Third: make bug reports cheap. The debug build has a pin button that writes one line of text with the coordinates, the heading and the build. I paste that line into the chat, an agent goes to that spot in a headless run, takes a picture and finds the cause. A river that stopped for 50 metres turned out to be two parallel lock channels in OpenStreetMap that the importer had chained into a loop.
    
    Fourth: the agent tests on the slow phone itself. An old Galaxy S8 from 2017 sits on adb next to the workstation, and "works on my desktop" does not count as done. An agent installs the build, waits until the phone has cooled to the same battery temperature, drives the same route on autopilot and reads the game's own frame log: frame times, CPU, GPU load, draw calls. Every new feature has a debug switch, so each one is measured on and off on the same build. Before launch that was 31 runs in one evening, and the verdict came as numbers: 60 fps held everywhere, the new chrome and lamps cost 0.14 fps, the new workshop scene halved the GPU load of the old one. Only one agent may hold the phone at a time.
    
    Where a human still had to play it. Green tests mean exactly what the tests check. On my own phone, right before launch, I tapped a settings row and nothing appeared, but the screen behind stopped scrolling: a page had opened invisibly and was swallowing every touch. It had been like that for a week, and no automated walk ever saw it, because their setup step happened to build that page first. Same story with a map picture that was drawn over a dialog, and numbers that sat a few pixels too high on a share card. None of that is "broken" to a test. All of it is obvious in ten seconds with the phone in your hand.
    
    So my honest summary: the agents are fast and thorough at what you ask them, and the proof culture matters more than the prompt. But somebody still has to play the thing on a real phone and ask the simple questions.
    
    Austria is free to play, the other three countries are a one-time country pack, no ads.
    https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.trundleway.game
    
    Happy to go into any of it: the port, the rules file, how I split work between agents, what it cost.

comments.author: Wooden-Motor4870
comments.body:
Cool !  
How did you generate realistic maps with terrain relief? Behind these simple graphics, I’m sure there’s some technology at work ;)

replies.author: Andy12100
replies.body:
Thanks! No AI-generated terrain, it's all open data plus a bake step:

Roads, towns and rivers come from OpenStreetMap. A script folds each motorway's two carriageways into one centre line, finds the interchanges and smooths the curves so a truck can actually drive them.

The hills are the Copernicus GLO-30 elevation model (free, 30 m resolution), resampled onto the game's own grid. Then the ground gets shaped to the roads: cuttings, embankments, river beds, bridges and tunnels where the road and the terrain disagree.

The trick that makes it playable: the map is compressed. Distances between cities are about 1:15, towns about 1:4, and the heights are scaled down too, otherwise Vienna to Budapest would take three hours and the Alps would be a wall. So it's the real shape of the country, not the real size.

The agents wrote the whole pipeline. The fun part is that real data has real surprises. For instance at one spot the river is drawn as two lines side by side on the map, one for big ships and one for small boats. My importer followed one line down and the other back up, so in the game the river just ended in a field and started again 50 metres later.
